section_new.excerpt: ## The accounting At each step, the offered traffic is split between legacy and target. The model serves up to each path's capacity: target_served = min(arrival * target_share * dt, target_capacity * dt) legacy_served = min(arrival * (1 - target_share) * dt, legacy_capacity * dt) rejected = offered - target_served - legacy_served The dual-write backlog grows with target throughput times the declared lag and drains at the reconciliation capacity: backlog += target_served * dual_write_lag backlog -= min(backlog, reconciliation_capacity * dt) Divergence accumulates when the backlog exceeds the drain capacity. It is a synthetic proxy, not a measured data-quality metric.
section_new.heading: The accounting

section_new.excerpt: ## Purpose and mission “Ten thousand users” is not a sufficient workload specification. A system may have ten thousand accounts and almost no concurrent work; another with the same account count may receive a short burst of writes against one state key. Architecture decisions need a model of **arrivals, logical operations, concurrency, resource demand, key skew and time**. A good model makes assumptions visible and can be disproved by real observations. This foundational chapter describes how to define those quantities and estimate offered work without converting user population into requests per second by an invented universal constant. The [V10 architecture requirement profile](../../v10-d

section_new.excerpt: ## Hard constraints versus preferences A hard constraint is a condition a candidate must satisfy. If candidate C exceeds a declared cost ceiling, C is eliminated even if it has the highest success rate. A soft constraint is a preference that can be traded. A non-quantitative constraint is a condition the model cannot measure, such as operability by the existing team or a regulatory approval. The V12 checkout record uses two hard quantitative constraints (cost and p95 latency) and one non-quantitative constraint (operability). C is eliminated by the cost and latency constraints. B and A both pass. B wins on success rate and cost per successful request; A wins on p95 latency but does not meet
section_new.heading: Hard constraints versus preferences

section_new.excerpt: ## A worked cross-chapter synthesis A synthetic checkout service receives 20 requests per second for 30 minutes after a five-minute warmup. Three candidates use the same arrivals, duration, seed scheme and metrics: - A: direct capacity with a one-second deadline and no retry budget; - B: a bounded queue, a two-second deadline and a small retry budget; - C: more servers, a slower mean service time and a higher unit cost. Under the declared assumptions, B succeeds on 0.9996 of offered requests with a 1.206-second p95 latency and 1.34 relative cost units per 1000 successes. A succeeds on 0.9218 with a 0.870-second p95 and 1.81 cost units. C succeeds on 0.9679 but exceeds the declared 3.0 cost a
section_new.heading: A worked cross-chapter synthesis

section_new.excerpt: ## Why reliability was not automatically improved In the Servlet model a thread can remain attached to a request while it waits on a downstream dependency. A downstream latency spike and repeated device retries can amplify open connections, threads, memory and scheduler pressure. A Netty event loop lowers the cost of *waiting connections*, but this trades straightforward per-request stacks for callback lifecycle state, context propagation and manual resource cleanup. Netflix describes difficult-to-debug **ByteBuf leaks, file-descriptor leaks and dropped responses** as possible failures of incomplete async error paths. These are publisher-identified failure classes, not a confirmed list of ev
section_new.heading: Why reliability was not automatically improved

items.question: What evidence must a V12 model contract attach to an input labeled measured?

section_new.excerpt: ## What replay proves Replay proves that the stored inputs, engine version and seed produce the stored metrics on the same platform family. It does not prove that the model is valid, that the inputs are measured or that the decision is correct. A replay that matches is a reproducibility check, not a truth check. Platform strings can differ across operating systems and Python builds. V12 stores the platform string and the Python version so a mismatch is visible. The engine's metrics are deterministic for the same inputs and seeds; the environment string is evidence, not a guarantee of bit-identical behavior on every platform.
section_new.heading: What replay proves

section_new.excerpt: ## How the contract is validated The V12 validator checks four things: 1. The object matches the strict JSON Schema for model specifications. 2. The identifier is unique and starts with tycho.model. 3. Every scenario that names the model resolves to this identifier. 4. Every parameter with evidence status measured has a source and a measurement record. The validator cannot check that a source actually supports a parameter. That is an editorial and review task. The contract only prevents an obvious mismatch between the label and the record.
section_new.heading: How the contract is validated

section_new.excerpt: ## Correlated inputs Independent draws are a modelling assumption, not a neutral default. In the modernization scenario, a longer dual-write lag plausibly coincides with a lower reconciliation capacity: the same operational pressure produces both. V12 declares a negative correlation of -0.4 between those inputs and labels the uncertainty method as a Gaussian copula. The engine's sampling applies the declared correlation to the input draws. It does not infer a correlation from data. A model that ignores a known correlation produces an output distribution that is too narrow and a decision that looks more certain than it is.
section_new.heading: Correlated inputs

section_new.excerpt: ## The reproducibility contract The V12 run record stores: - model and scenario SHA-256; - engine name and version; - seed base and replication count; - an input hash over the model, scenario and engine version; - Python and platform strings; - the invocation; - metrics, convergence, uncertainty and sensitivity; - a result hash over the substantive fields. The model and scenario files are the canonical inputs. The run record is derived. A change to either input invalidates the run until it is regenerated.
section_new.heading: The reproducibility contract

section_new.excerpt: ## A stopping rule A practical stopping rule is: 1. Run a pilot with at least 10 replications. 2. Estimate the standard error of the primary metric. 3. Compute the required n for the target relative error. 4. Run to that n or to a declared budget, whichever is smaller. 5. Record the achieved error and whether the target was met. V12 does not adapt n during a run. The scenario declares the replication count, and the run reports the achieved error. This keeps the result reproducible; an adaptive stopping rule would need its own seeded decision log.

section_new.excerpt: # Event ordering and timeouts **Question.** Which event-ordering and timeout rules must be fixed so that two runs with the same seed produce the same outcome? **Short answer.** A discrete-event engine must define a total order over events, schedule timeouts explicitly, cancel stale events and record how a retry resets a deadline. V12 uses (time, priority, insertion sequence) and a per-attempt timeout event.
section_new.heading: Event ordering and timeouts

section_new.excerpt: ## Retry amplification If every request is attempted 1.05 times on average, the service load is 5% higher than the offered load. If every request is attempted three times, the load can be three times higher. The retry amplification metric is total attempts divided by offered requests. V12 reports it for every discrete-event run. The A/B/C comparison shows the difference: - A has no retry budget: retry amplification 1.000, timeout rate 0.0778, success 0.9218. - B has three attempts with exponential backoff and full jitter: retry amplification 1.004, timeout rate 0.0041, success 0.9996. - C has two attempts with linear backoff: retry amplification 1.079, timeout rate 0.111, success 0.9679. That approach assumes the future distribution resembles the input estimates. Actual datasets can be very different months later, or a small number of valid IDs can receive disproportionate traffic. Both extremes matter. An oversized partition may

section_new.excerpt: ## Standard error For n independent replications with sample standard deviation s, the standard error of the mean is: se = s / sqrt(n) A 95% confidence interval under a normal approximation is: mean +/- 1.96 * se The interval is narrower when n is larger or the output is less variable. It does not become more valid if the replications are correlated or the output distribution is heavy-tailed. V12 uses the normal approximation across replications. For 30 replications the approximation is reasonable for a bounded metric such as success rate. For a heavy-tailed latency, it can understate the tail uncertainty. The decision record records that limit.
section_new.heading: Standard error

section_new.excerpt: ## JCGM 100 and uncertainty language JCGM 100 describes a measurement result as a measured value plus an uncertainty, with a coverage interval at a stated coverage probability. It distinguishes Type A and Type B uncertainty components and shows how to combine them. V12 uses the vocabulary but not the full method. A uniform range in a scenario is not a Type A or Type B component. It is an assumed input range. A confidence interval across replications is a sampling interval, not a metrological coverage interval. The page says so to prevent a reader from treating a synthetic interval as a calibrated uncertainty budget.
section_new.heading: JCGM 100 and uncertainty language

A full scan returning a single row cost the same as a point lookup; quotas remained static while workload skew and hotspots evolved. The Redis round trip added a reliability dependency, and query nodes did not possess current health signals for all storage partitions. The authors report that this approach **did not
section_new.heading: Why the first idea failed in production

items.question: How does the V12 quadratic sensitivity screen differ from a full Sobol analysis?

section_new.excerpt: ## Sensitivity and uncertainty The candidate B sensitivity screen reports arrival rate first-order 0.361 and total-order 0.464, service mean first-order 0.536 and total-order 0.639. The screen is a quadratic approximation over 48 rows. It says service time explains more of the fitted variance in the sampled range. It does not prove that service time is the dominant production factor. The sensitivity scenario is converged at a 0.00016 relative error. A separate two-replication convergence-stress run is insufficient-sample at 0.032. The decision record does not use the sensitivity ranking to support a production claim; it uses it to identify what to measure first.
section_new.heading: Sensitivity and uncertainty

section_new.excerpt: ## Scope The engine implements: - a fixed-step stock-and-flow backlog model with exact request conservation; - a discrete-event checkout model with capacity, queueing, timeouts, retries and backpressure; - a staged modernization model with dual-write lag, reconciliation and rollback; - seeded replications and Monte Carlo aggregation; - a quadratic response-surface sensitivity screen; - canonical JSON hashing and a replay command. It does not implement a general-purpose simulation language, distributed execution, a graphical interface, a database or a production scheduler. A model family that needs a new mechanism gets a new explicit contract, not an unrecorded engine extension.
